clinicalPearls: Suspect in a young patient (especially female on estrogen-containing contraception or postpartum) with new headache plus seizure, focal deficit, or altered consciousness
Headache is the most common presenting symptom and can be subacute, progressive, or thunderclap-like, sometimes mimicking idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Papilledema from raised intracranial pressure may occur even without a clear focal deficit
Deficits often do not respect a single arterial territory and may be bilateral or migrate, reflecting venous rather than arterial infarction
Hemorrhagic venous infarcts are common and should not by themselves prompt withholding anticoagulation
Seizures, especially with focal onset, occur more frequently than in typical arterial ischemic stroke
A normal non-contrast CT does not exclude the diagnosis; dedicated venous imaging is required
Consider an underlying prothrombotic, infectious, or inflammatory trigger in every confirmed case
harrison.pathophysiology: Thrombosis of a dural venous sinus or cortical vein obstructs cerebral venous drainage, raising venous and capillary pressure. This leads to impaired CSF resorption with intracranial hypertension, and can progress to vasogenic edema, venous congestion, and eventually venous infarction with secondary hemorrhage. Because venous drainage territories overlap and are variable between individuals, resulting deficits are often atypical for a single vascular distribution.
additionalDifferentials: Primary or metastatic brain tumor with mass effect
infectionMimics: Septic (infective) intracranial venous sinus thrombosis from adjacent otitis, mastoiditis, or sinusitis
nonInfectiousMimics: Subarachnoid or intraparenchymal hemorrhage from other causes
additionalInvestigations: MR venography or CT venography — confirms sinus/cortical vein occlusion and is the primary diagnostic study
Non-contrast head CT — may show hyperdense sinus or hemorrhagic venous infarct but can be normal early on
MRI brain with venous sequences — detects venous infarction, edema, and hemorrhage better than CT
D-dimer — supportive if elevated but a normal level does not exclude the diagnosis, especially with isolated headache
Coagulation and thrombophilia workup — evaluates for underlying prothrombotic states once acute treatment is underway
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure — assesses for raised intracranial pressure and excludes infectious causes when imaging is inconclusive
Ophthalmologic exam for papilledema — assesses risk of visual loss from raised intracranial pressure
Screening for precipitating factors (pregnancy/postpartum status, oral contraceptive or hormonal therapy use, malignancy, recent infection or dehydration)
redFlags: Rapidly declining consciousness or signs of impending herniation
New or worsening papilledema with visual field loss threatening vision
Extensive bilateral hemorrhagic venous infarction on imaging
Status epilepticus or recurrent seizures at presentation
Clinical deterioration despite anticoagulation, suggesting need for endovascular or surgical intervention
pitfalls: Dismissing headache as migraine or tension-type without considering CVST in at-risk patients (pregnancy, postpartum, hormonal contraception, thrombophilia)
Withholding anticoagulation because of hemorrhagic venous infarction, which is generally still an indication for treatment rather than a contraindication
Relying on a normal non-contrast CT to exclude the diagnosis instead of obtaining dedicated venous imaging
Attributing bilateral or non-arterial-territory deficits to a psychiatric or functional cause rather than pursuing venous imaging
harrison.prognosis: Most patients who receive timely anticoagulation have a favorable outcome with good functional recovery, though a minority develop persistent neurological deficits, chronic intracranial hypertension, or, rarely, death from extensive venous infarction or herniation. Recurrence risk depends on the presence and persistence of underlying prothrombotic risk factors.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Cerebrovascular Diseases (Cerebral Venous Thrombosis)
management: Prompt anticoagulation with therapeutic heparin followed by an oral anticoagulant, continued even when a haemorrhagic venous infarct is present.
Endovascular thrombectomy or thrombolysis reserved for patients who deteriorate despite adequate anticoagulation.
Management of raised intracranial pressure with acetazolamide, therapeutic lumbar puncture, and decompressive craniectomy for impending herniation.
Antiseizure medication for patients who have had seizures.
Identification and removal of precipitants, including stopping oestrogen-containing contraception and treating any underlying infection, with a thrombophilia and malignancy work-up.
Duration of anticoagulation guided by whether the event was provoked or unprovoked and by any identified thrombophilia.
Multidisciplinary stroke and neurology care, with escalation for declining consciousness or extensive venous infarction.

valueTables.title: Differential diagnosis of cerebral venous thrombosis

cells.text: Headache and papilloedema with patent sinuses
Infarct in an arterial territory, sudden onset
Transverse sinus hypoplasia, arachnoid granulations, flow artefact
Combine MRV sequences or CTV; DSA if unclear

valueTables.title: Treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis

cells.text: {{hy:Acute phase, even with haemorrhagic venous infarct}}
Preferred by ESO 2017 over unfractionated heparin
Usually 3 to 12 months, INR 2.0 to 3.0; longer with APS or thrombophilia
Alternative to warfarin after acute phase
Dabigatran similar to warfarin in a 120-patient trial
TO-ACT trial showed no clear benefit in severe CVT
Impending herniation from large infarct or haematoma

valueTables.footnote: Complete recovery in 57% to 86%; mortality 5% to 18% across the review's figures.

valueTables.title: Oral contraceptives: contraindications and disease risk

cells.text: Previous thromboembolic event or stroke; history of estrogen-dependent tumor; active liver disease; pregnancy; undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding; hypertriglyceridemia; women over 35 who smoke heavily
Hypertension; women on anticonvulsant therapy; women after bariatric (malabsorptive) surgery
Increased in smokers over 35; no relation to progestin type
Relative risk 1.8 in current users and 1.2 in previous users

Relative risk about 4; may be higher with third-generation progestin, drospirenone, and the patch; compounded by obesity (tenfold risk compared with nonobese non-users); markedly increased with factor V Leiden or prothrombin-gene mutations
Slight increase; relation to migraine headache unclear
Relative risk about 13 to 15; synergistic with prothrombin-gene mutation
May increase risk in carriers of BRCA1 and possibly BRCA2
